title: Minimum Spanning Tree — Prim
tagline: Grow the tree one cheapest frontier edge at a time — MST via a priority queue.

intuition.analogy: Growing a tree from a seed: at each step you extend it by the cheapest branch reaching a node not yet in the tree. The tree expands outward like Dijkstra, but you compare single edge weights instead of accumulated distances.
paragraphs: Prim's algorithm builds the MST by growing a single tree from a starting vertex. It keeps a frontier of edges crossing from the tree to the rest, and always absorbs the cheapest such edge.
A min-priority-queue of candidate edges (or of nodes keyed by their cheapest connecting edge) makes choosing that edge efficient. When a node is pulled in, its new edges to outside nodes are pushed.
Prim shines on dense graphs (compared to Kruskal), and its structure closely mirrors Dijkstra — the only difference is what the key represents (edge weight vs path distance).
intuition.keyIdea: Maintain the cheapest edge from the growing tree to each outside node; repeatedly absorb the global minimum.

steps.title: Seed the tree
steps.detail: Start from any vertex; push its incident edges into a min-heap.

steps.title: Absorb the cheapest frontier edge
steps.detail: Pop the minimum edge. If it leads to a new vertex, add that vertex (and the edge) to the tree.

steps.title: Expand the frontier
steps.detail: Push the new vertex's edges to outside nodes. Repeat until all vertices are in the tree.

codes.source:
import heapq

def prim(n, adj):                    # adj[u] = [(v, w), ...]
    in_tree = [False] * n
    pq = [(0, 0)]                    # (weight, node)
    cost = 0
    while pq:
        w, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        if in_tree[u]:
            continue
        in_tree[u] = True
        cost += w
        for v, wt in adj[u]:
            if not in_tree[v]:
                heapq.heappush(pq, (wt, v))
    return cost

complexity.timeReason: Each edge may be pushed once; heap ops cost log V.

pitfalls: Skip popped vertices already in the tree (stale heap entries).
Adding edge weights, not accumulated distances — that's the Dijkstra difference.
For very dense graphs, an O(V²) array-based Prim can beat the heap version.

dryRun.clickMoment: C is reached via B at weight 1, beating the direct A-C edge of 3. Prim always grabs the cheapest way to extend the current tree, never the cheapest edge globally.

problems.title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
problems.statement: Minimum total distance to connect all points.
problems.hint: Prim is great here since the graph is implicitly complete.

approach: Prim grows the tree from one vertex, always adding the cheapest edge crossing to an unvisited point. With a complete Manhattan graph a min-heap drives the selection.
Pop the nearest unvisited point, add its weight, then push its distances to remaining points.

problems.title: Connecting Cities With Minimum Cost
problems.statement: Connect all cities minimally or return -1.

approach: Build an adjacency list and run Prim from city 1, repeatedly adding the cheapest edge to a new city via a min-heap.
If we cannot include all n cities, the graph is disconnected → -1.

problems.title: Optimize Water Distribution
problems.hint: Virtual node for wells, then Prim.

approach: Add a virtual node 0 connected to each house by an edge equal to that house's well cost. Then a spanning tree of this augmented graph is the cheapest water plan.
Run Prim from node 0 with a min-heap over both pipe edges and well edges.

problems.title: Minimum Spanning Tree
problems.statement: Compute MST weight of a weighted graph.

approach: Generic MST via Prim: start anywhere, keep a min-heap of edges crossing the cut, and pull the lightest one that reaches a new vertex.
Return the accumulated weight once all vertices are included.

problems.title: Network Build-out Cost
problems.statement: Cheapest way to make a network fully connected.

approach: The cheapest network build-out connecting all sites is exactly an MST. Prim accumulates the minimum total edge weight that keeps the network connected.
Use a visited array plus a min-heap; each site joins via its cheapest crossing edge.
